source: Out of the trunk, the branches grow; out of them, the twigs. So, in productive subjects, grow the chapters.

The crotch alluded to on a previous page deserves independent mention. It is a notched stick of a peculiar form, some two feet in length, which is perpendicularly inserted into the starboard gunwale near the bow, for the purpose of furnishing a rest for the wooden extremity of the harpoon, whose other naked, barbed end slopingly projects from the prow. Thereby the weapon is instantly at hand to its hurler, who snatches it up as readily from its rest as a backwoodsman swings his rifle from the wall. It is customary to have two harpoons reposing in the crotch, respectively called the first and second irons.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected with the line; the object being this: to dart them both, if possible, one instantly after the other into the same whale; so that if, in the coming drag, one should draw out, the other may still retain a hold. It is a doubling of the chances. But it very often happens that owing to the instantaneous, violent, convulsive running of the whale upon receiving the first iron, it becomes impossible for the harpooneer, however lightning-like in his movements, to pitch the second iron into him. Nevertheless, as the second iron is already connected with the line, and the line is running, hence that weapon must, at all events, be anticipatingly tossed out of the boat, somehow and somewhere; else the most terrible jeopardy would involve all hands. Tumbled into the water, it accordingly is in such cases; the spare coils of box line (mentioned in a preceding chapter) making this feat, in most instances, prudently practicable. But this critical act is not always unattended with the saddest and most fatal casualties.

Furthermore: you must know that when the second iron is thrown overboard, it thenceforth becomes a dangling, sharp-edged terror, skittishly curvetting about both boat and whale, entangling the lines, or cutting them, and making a prodigious sensation in all directions. Nor, in general, is it possible to secure it again until the whale is fairly captured and a corpse.

Consider, now, how it must be in the case of four boats all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand concurring accidents of such an audacious enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be simultaneously dangling about him. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to bend on to the line should the first one be ineffectually darted without recovery. All these particulars are faithfully narrated here, as they will not fail to elucidate several most important, however intricate passages, in scenes hereafter to be painted.

modern_en.title: Chapter 63 — The Crotch
paragraphs: The branches grow out of the trunk, and the twigs out of the branches. In the same way, in productive subjects, the chapters grow.

The crotch mentioned on a previous page deserves a mention of its own. It is a notched stick of a peculiar shape, some two feet long, which is inserted upright into the starboard gunwale near the bow, to provide a rest for the wooden end of the harpoon, whose other, naked, barbed end projects at a slant from the prow. In this way the weapon is instantly at hand for its thrower, who snatches it up from its rest as readily as a backwoodsman swings his rifle down from the wall. It is customary to have two harpoons resting in the crotch, called respectively the first and second irons.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected with the line; the object being this: to dart them both, if possible, one instantly after the other into the same whale, so that if, in the coming drag, one should pull out, the other may still keep its hold. It is a doubling of the chances. But it very often happens that, owing to the instantaneous, violent, convulsive running of the whale on receiving the first iron, it becomes impossible for the harpooner, however lightning-quick his movements, to pitch the second iron into him. Nevertheless, since the second iron is already connected with the line, and the line is running, that weapon must at all events be tossed out of the boat in advance, somehow and somewhere; otherwise all hands would be in the most terrible danger. So in such cases it is tumbled into the water, the spare coils of box line (mentioned in a preceding chapter) making this feat, in most instances, prudently possible. But this critical act is not always free of the saddest and most fatal accidents.

Something else you should know: once the second iron has been thrown overboard, it turns into a dangling, sharp-edged menace, darting skittishly about both boat and whale, fouling the lines or slicing them, and causing a tremendous stir in every direction. And as a rule it cannot be secured again until the whale has been properly caught and is a corpse.

Consider, now, how it must be when four boats are all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when, owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand coinciding accidents of such a daring enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be dangling about him at once. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to bend on to the line should the first one be darted without effect and not recovered. All these particulars are faithfully set down here, as they will not fail to shed light on several most important, however intricate, passages in scenes to be painted later.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 63 — Klosen
paragraphs: Grenene vokser ud af stammen, og kviste ud af grenene. På samme måde vokser kapitlerne i frugtbare emner.

Gaflen, der blev nævnt på en tidligere side, fortjener en omtale for sig. Det er en kærvet stok af ejendommelig form, omkring to fod lang, som sættes lodret ind i styrbords essing nær stævnen for at give støtte til harpunens trædel, hvis anden, nøgne, modhagede ende rager skråt ud fra forstavnen. På den måde er våbnet øjeblikkelig ved hånden for sin kaster, som griber det op fra dets støtte lige så let, som en skovbo svinger sin riffel ned fra væggen. Det er sædvane at have to harpuner hvilende i gaflen, kaldet henholdsvis første og andet jern.

Men disse to harpuner er hver med sin egen snor begge forbundet med linen; hensigten er denne: at kaste dem begge, om muligt, den ene lige efter den anden i den samme hval, så hvis den ene i det kommende træk skulle rive sig løs, kan den anden stadig holde fast. Det er en fordobling af chancerne. Men det sker meget ofte, at det på grund af hvalens øjeblikkelige, voldsomme, krampagtige løb, når den får det første jern, bliver umuligt for harpunéren, hvor lynsnare hans bevægelser end er, at kaste det andet jern i den. Ikke desto mindre må det våben, eftersom det andet jern allerede er forbundet med linen, og linen løber, under alle omstændigheder på forhånd smides ud af båden, på en eller anden måde og et eller andet sted; ellers ville alle mand være i den frygteligste fare. Så i sådanne tilfælde væltes det i vandet, idet de ekstra tørn af kasselinen (nævnt i et tidligere kapitel) i de fleste tilfælde gør dette kunststykke forsigtigt muligt. Men denne kritiske handling er ikke altid fri for de sørgeligste og dødeligste ulykker.

Noget andet, du bør vide: Når det andet jern først er kastet overbord, bliver det til en dinglende, skarpkantet trussel, der farer skræmt rundt om både båd og hval, sammenfiltrer linerne eller skærer dem over og skaber et vældigt røre til alle sider. Og som regel kan det ikke fastgøres igen, før hvalen er ordentligt fanget og er et lig.

Tænk dig nu, hvordan det må være, når fire både alle angriber én usædvanlig stærk, rap og kløgtig hval; når der på grund af disse egenskaber hos ham, såvel som de tusind sammenfaldende tilfældigheder i en så dristig bedrift, kan dingle otte eller ti løse andre jern omkring ham på én gang. For naturligvis er hver båd forsynet med flere harpuner til at slå på linen, hvis den første skulle blive kastet uden virkning og ikke fås tilbage. Alle disse enkeltheder er trofast nedskrevet her, da de ikke vil undlade at kaste lys over flere højst vigtige, om end indviklede, passager i scener, der skal males senere.
